tagline: A desert climb through limestone country to spring-fed falls
intro: The Guadalupe Back Country Scenic Byway begins twelve miles north of Carlsbad and climbs about 3,000 feet from the Chihuahuan Desert into the Guadalupe Mountains. The terrain quickly becomes rugged, with pale limestone outcrops, prickly pear and sotol, and wild caves beneath the surface. The Guadalupe Ranger District occupies an exposed part of the Capitan Reef, a Permian barrier that partly enclosed the Delaware Sea.

NM 137’s approach changed during the Brantley Dam project, when both it and US 285 were rerouted. The older McMillan Reservoir had been filling with silt, and a 1964 study identified inadequate spillway capacity and a risk of failure at both McMillan and Avalon dams. Congress approved the new project in 1972; dam construction began in 1984, and concrete work finished in autumn 1987.

From US 285 north of Carlsbad, NM 137 heads west toward the mountains. Sitting Bull Falls is a separate excursion from the highway, with a short path from parking to the falls viewing area. Farther exploration along NM 137 reaches Five Points Vista, with views of the Guadalupe Mountains and their western Rim. The full state highway continues to the Texas line, becoming Dog Canyon Road as it enters Guadalupe Mountains National Park.
notice: Prickly pear and sotol grow in patches among cream-colored limestone outcrops.

moments.title: Brantley Dam
moments.text: Brantley Dam combines a concrete center with earth-fill wings on the Pecos River. Its construction changed transport routes as well as water storage: US 285 and NM 137 were rerouted, and the Santa Fe Railway was realigned. Work on the dam began in 1984. After the concrete work finished in autumn 1987, the Pecos was diverted through the new floodgates. The resulting lake serves irrigation and flood control, and part of the dam and surrounding land belongs to Brantley Lake State Park. The concrete spillway has six radial gates; earth-fill wings extend to either side of the central structure.

moments.title: Sitting Bull Falls
moments.text: Spring water feeds Sitting Bull Falls, dropping 150 feet into a pool below. Above the drop, water passes through streams and pools; below it, most disappears into gravel or cracks in the rock. It reappears farther down the canyon or joins the Pecos Valley’s underground water supply. The picnic area includes stone buildings constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1940. Several shelters were repaired after a wildfire damaged the area in 2011. A short accessible path leads from the parking lot to the viewing area, with additional hiking trails in the recreation area.
moments.notice: Notice the CCC stone buildings in the parking and picnic area.

moments.title: Five Points Vista
moments.text: Five Points Vista overlooks the Guadalupe Mountains and the Rim, a cliff 1,500 to 2,000 feet high along the range’s western edge. The trip west from Carlsbad along NM 137 is approximately 50 miles. The surrounding Guadalupe Ranger District forms the back reef of the northern Capitan Reef. That Permian reef partly enclosed the Delaware Sea. The district changes from steep-walled southern canyons to rolling hills and smaller canyons draining east toward the Pecos valley. The Guadalupe area became part of Lincoln National Forest in 1917, when the Alamo National Forest was dissolved.
moments.notice: The Rim marks the western edge of the Guadalupe range.

practical: Sitting Bull Falls: The entry gate closes at 3:30 p.m.; the site closes at 4 p.m. Day use only, with no overnight camping. (checked 2026-10-11)
